questions.stem: Which statement best describes a renewable resource?
options: One that is made only by human industry and does not occur naturally in ecosystems
One that is typically replenished within years to decades, such as water or timber
One that forms over millions of years and cannot be replaced once it has been used
One that can never run out, however quickly people harvest it from the environment
questions.explanation: Renewable resources are replenished on timescales of years to decades, and they include harvestable resources and ecosystem services. They can still be depleted if they are used faster than they are replenished.

questions.stem: A student lists resources taken from Western Australian landscapes. Which one is a harvestable renewable resource?
options: Timber from a plantation
Iron ore from a pit
Natural gas from a field
Gold from a quartz vein
questions.explanation: Harvestable renewable resources include water, biota such as timber and fish, and some energy resources. Iron ore, natural gas and gold form over geological timescales and are non-renewable.

questions.stem: Water drawn from a river for irrigation is classed as a renewable resource mainly because:
options: it is formed slowly from minerals in the river bed over millions of years
it cannot be polluted or wasted, so its supply stays constant whatever the use
it is created by plants during photosynthesis in the forests of the catchment
it is replenished by the water cycle, through rainfall and runoff, within years
questions.explanation: Fresh water is continually replenished as the Sun drives evaporation, precipitation and runoff. It is renewable on years-to-decades timescales, but the rate of supply can still limit how much can be used.

questions.stem: Food, fresh water and timber obtained from ecosystems are examples of which type of ecosystem service?
options: Recreational services
Provisioning services
Regulating services
Supporting services
questions.explanation: Provisioning services are the products people obtain directly from ecosystems. Regulating services, such as carbon sequestration, control environmental conditions.

questions.stem: A mangrove forest stores large amounts of carbon in its waterlogged sediments. Which type of ecosystem service is this?
options: A provisioning service
A supporting service
A harvesting service
A regulating service
questions.explanation: Carbon sequestration removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and helps control climate, so it is a regulating service. Nothing is harvested or taken from the forest.

questions.stem: Soil organisms break down leaf litter and release nitrogen and phosphorus that plants then take up. How is this service classed?
options: A supporting service, because it cycles nutrients
A provisioning service, because it produces food for the soil organisms themselves
A regulating service, because it controls the climate of the forest floor
A harvestable resource, because people can collect the nutrients directly
questions.explanation: Nutrient cycling is a supporting service, along with air and water cycling. It is not harvested directly, but production of food, water and timber depends on it.

questions.stem: Vegetation around a wetland cools nearby air through evapotranspiration and stores carbon in its wood and soil. Both of these are:
options: regulating services: climate control and carbon sequestration
provisioning services: supply of cool air and supply of wood for fuel
supporting services: soil formation and the cycling of nutrients
harvestable resources, because people can collect both directly
questions.explanation: Climate control and carbon sequestration are the regulating services named in the syllabus. Supporting services are the cycling of nutrients, air and water that underpin the others.

questions.stem: Why are supporting services described as underpinning all the other ecosystem services?
options: They maintain the cycling of nutrients, air and water on which food, water and timber depend
They are the only services that people can harvest directly and sell for a profit
They operate only in farmland, where they support crops grown for human food
They are provided by human infrastructure such as dams rather than by ecosystems
questions.explanation: Provisioning services such as crops and timber can only be produced if nutrients, water and gases keep cycling through the ecosystem. That is why supporting services are seen as the base of the others.

questions.stem: A forested catchment is cleared for grazing. Which list correctly pairs each lost service with its type?
options: Timber: provisioning; carbon storage: regulating; nutrient cycling: supporting
Timber: regulating; carbon storage: supporting; nutrient cycling: provisioning
Timber: supporting; carbon storage: provisioning; nutrient cycling: regulating
Timber: provisioning; carbon storage: supporting; nutrient cycling: regulating
questions.explanation: Timber is a product taken from the ecosystem, carbon storage helps regulate climate, and nutrient cycling supports all other services. The last list wrongly swaps the regulating and supporting services.

questions.stem: Seagrass meadows off the Western Australian coast supply fish later caught by fishers and trap carbon in their sediments. Which pair of services do they provide?
options: Provisioning (fish) and regulating (carbon sequestration)
Supporting (fish) and provisioning (carbon sequestration)
Regulating (fish) and supporting (carbon sequestration)
Provisioning (fish) and supporting (carbon sequestration)
questions.explanation: Fish caught for food are a provisioning service. Trapping carbon is carbon sequestration, which the syllabus classes as a regulating service.

questions.stem: Why can a renewable resource such as a fish stock still be depleted?
options: Fish stocks are renewable only in fresh water, so marine stocks always decline
Depletion happens only to non-renewable resources, so a fish stock cannot decline
If it is harvested faster than it is replenished, the stock declines over time
Renewable resources are replaced only once, so a second harvest removes them for good
questions.explanation: Being renewable means a resource is replenished, not that it is unlimited. When harvest exceeds the replenishment rate the stock shrinks, and it can collapse if this continues.

questions.stem: A renewable resource is being used sustainably when:
options: it is harvested as fast as possible before it can be lost to natural causes
it is harvested only until the stock has fallen to half its original size
it is harvested at any rate, because renewable resources always recover
it is harvested no faster than it is replenished, so the stock does not decline
questions.explanation: A sustainable rate of use keeps the stock from declining over time, which means harvest must not exceed replenishment. Harvesting faster can deplete even a renewable resource.

questions.stem: A fish stock of 40 000 t replenishes by about 15% of its size each year. What is the largest annual catch that would keep the stock stable?
questions.explanation: Replenishment is 15% of 40 000 t = 6000 t per year. Catching more than this reduces the stock, and 34 000 t is the stock that would remain after a 6000 t catch.

questions.stem: A 12 000 ha pine plantation is grown on a 30-year rotation. To supply a steady yield indefinitely, about how much can be clear-felled and replanted each year?
options: 360 ha
30 ha
400 ha
questions.explanation: With a 30-year rotation, one-thirtieth of the area can be harvested each year: 12 000 ÷ 30 = 400 ha. Each block then has 30 years to regrow before it is cut again.

questions.stem: An aquifer is recharged by about 50 GL of rainfall each year, but 70 GL is pumped from it each year. What will happen if this continues?
options: Storage will stay the same, because the aquifer refills faster as it is pumped
Storage will fall at first but recover once the water has been used on crops
Storage will fall and the water table will drop, so the use is not sustainable
Storage will rise and the water table will climb, so pumping must be increased
questions.explanation: Extraction exceeds recharge by 20 GL a year, so the aquifer loses that much stored water every year. Sustainable use keeps extraction at or below the rate of recharge.

questions.stem: An old-growth forest holds a huge volume of timber but regrows over centuries. A smaller plantation holds less timber but regrows in 30 years. Which statement is best?
options: Both can be harvested at the same rate, because both are renewable timber resources
The plantation cannot be harvested sustainably, because it holds less timber in total
The forest's large stock does not allow a high harvest rate, because it replenishes slowly
The forest can be harvested faster than the plantation because it holds much more timber
questions.explanation: A sustainable rate depends on both abundance and how readily a resource is replenished. A slowly replenished resource can sustain only a low harvest rate, however large its stock.

questions.stem: Total pumping from a regional aquifer is well below its total recharge, yet the water table has fallen sharply around one town where many bores are clustered. What does this show?
options: Use can be sustainable at a regional scale but unsustainable at a local scale
The regional recharge estimate must be wrong, since water tables never vary locally
Groundwater always flows quickly enough to refill any local drawdown within days
The town's bores must be drawing from a non-renewable source of fossil water only
questions.explanation: Groundwater moves slowly, so concentrated pumping creates a local cone of depression even when regional totals balance. Sustainable use has to be judged at local, regional and global scales.

questions.stem: Orange roughy, a deep-sea fish, lives for over a century and breeds only late in life. Why were stocks quickly over-fished?
options: Slow growth and late breeding meant replenishment was far slower than the catch
Its large population meant fishers took too few fish to cover the costs of fishing
It breeds many times each year, so the stock grew too fast for fishers to manage
Deep-sea fish are not renewable, so any catch at all is bound to wipe them out
questions.explanation: A species that grows slowly and breeds late replenishes very slowly, so only a small catch is sustainable. Catches set as if the stock were fast-growing removed fish far faster than they were replaced.

questions.stem: A fish stock is fished down to a small fraction of its original size. Why does this lower the catch it can sustain in future?
options: Fishing has no effect on replenishment, which depends only on ocean temperature
Fewer breeding adults produce fewer young, so the replenishment rate itself falls
Smaller stocks always grow faster, so fishers must catch more to keep them stable
The remaining fish stop breeding entirely until the stock is fully replaced by stocking
questions.explanation: Replenishment depends on the number of breeding adults. A depleted stock produces fewer young each year, so its sustainable yield is lower and recovery can take many years.

questions.stem: Managers of a lobster fishery count young lobsters settling on collectors each year and use these counts to set catch limits several years ahead. Why does this help sustainable use?
options: It allows fishers to catch the young lobsters before natural predators take them
It replaces the need for any catch limits, since the collectors breed new lobsters
It measures replenishment of the stock before those lobsters reach legal size
It measures the number of adult lobsters already caught in the previous season
questions.explanation: Counting young recruits shows how many lobsters will join the fishable stock in coming years. Monitoring replenishment lets managers adjust harvest so it does not exceed what the stock can replace.

questions.stem: Why do fisheries managers use models alongside annual monitoring of catches and stock surveys?
options: To guarantee the exact size of next year's stock, so no catch limits are needed
To increase the replenishment rate of the stock by predicting where fish will swim
To predict how the stock will respond to different catch levels and set limits
To replace field data entirely, since models are always more accurate than surveys
questions.explanation: Models combine monitoring data to forecast stock size under different harvest rates, so limits can be set within the replenishment rate. They rely on data and assumptions and carry uncertainty.

questions.stem: Southern bluefin tuna migrate across the waters of several countries and the high seas. Why must their harvest be managed at a global scale?
options: Each country's waters contain a separate stock that replenishes independently
Tuna replenish only in Australian waters, so other countries do not affect them
Global management lets every country catch as much as it chooses each year
Catches in any one region reduce the single shared stock that all regions rely on
questions.explanation: A migratory species forms one stock across many jurisdictions, so its sustainable yield can only be kept by agreed limits on the total catch. Sustainable use must be considered at local, regional and global scales.

questions.stem: What does the efficiency of an energy technology, such as a solar panel, measure?
options: The cost of each unit of energy it produces, including building and maintenance
The time it takes to repay the energy that was used to manufacture the device
The percentage of the input energy that is converted into useful output energy
The total amount of energy the technology produces over a full year of operation
questions.explanation: Efficiency is useful energy out divided by energy in, usually as a percentage. Total yearly output depends on efficiency but also on the size of the device and how much of the time it operates.

questions.stem: The cost-effective use of renewable energy is limited mainly by the efficiency of technologies to:
options: collect, store and transfer the energy
create new energy from nothing at all
increase the total energy the Sun emits
convert electricity back into sunlight
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created, so what limits renewable energy is how much of it can be captured, stored for when it is needed and delivered to users. Losses at each step raise the cost per unit of useful energy.

questions.stem: Sunlight of 1000 W per square metre falls on a 1.5 m² solar panel with an efficiency of 20%. What is its electrical power output?
questions.explanation: Incident power is 1000 × 1.5 = 1500 W, and 20% of that is 300 W. The other 80% is reflected or turned into heat in the panel.

questions.stem: Solar panels convert 20% of sunlight to electricity. The electricity is stored in a battery that returns 90% of what it receives, then transmitted with 95% efficiency. What percentage of the sunlight is delivered?
options: About 5%
About 17%
About 20%
About 86%
questions.explanation: Efficiencies multiply along a chain: 0.20 × 0.90 × 0.95 = 0.171, or about 17%. Subtracting the percentage losses from 20% gives 5%, which is not how efficiencies combine.

questions.stem: The power available in the wind is proportional to the cube of wind speed. If the wind speed at a turbine doubles from 5 m/s to 10 m/s, the available power:
options: doubles
increases four times
stays the same
increases eight times
questions.explanation: Doubling the speed multiplies power by 2³ = 8. This is why turbines are placed on exposed ridges and coasts and on tall towers, where winds are stronger.

questions.stem: Why can no wind turbine extract all of the kinetic energy of the wind passing through it?
options: Wind energy is mostly heat, which turbine blades cannot convert to motion
The air must keep moving past the blades, which caps extraction at about 59%
The blades create new energy that cancels out the energy taken from the wind
The air stops completely at the blades, so the turbine stalls if it takes more
questions.explanation: If all the kinetic energy were removed the air would stop and no more air could flow through the rotor. The theoretical maximum, the Betz limit, is about 59%, and real turbines capture less because of further losses.

questions.stem: A 50 MW wind farm generates 175 200 MWh in a year of 8760 hours. What is its capacity factor?
questions.explanation: At full output all year it would generate 50 × 8760 = 438 000 MWh. Actual output ÷ maximum = 175 200 ÷ 438 000 = 0.40, or 40%, because the wind does not always blow strongly.

questions.stem: Why does relying heavily on solar and wind electricity add to the cost of a power system?
options: They can operate only when connected directly to a coal-fired power station
Their output varies with weather and time of day, so storage or backup is needed
Their output is constant day and night, so excess electricity is always wasted
They need fuel deliveries every day, which raises the cost of each unit generated
questions.explanation: Solar and wind are intermittent. Matching supply to demand needs storage, such as batteries or pumped hydro, or other generation, and storage itself loses some energy and costs money to build.

questions.stem: Why is electricity from a remote wind farm transmitted over long distances at very high voltage?
options: A higher voltage increases the power generated by the turbines at the wind farm
A higher voltage stops electricity leaking out of the cables into the ground
A higher voltage lets the cables carry energy faster than the speed of light
A higher voltage carries the same power at lower current, reducing heating losses
questions.explanation: Resistive losses in a line depend on the square of the current. Raising the voltage lowers the current for the same power, so less energy is lost as heat along the line.

questions.stem: Why are large solar farms not always built in the sunniest, most remote desert areas?
options: Desert heat increases panel efficiency so much that the panels soon wear out
Solar panels work only near the coast, where sea breezes keep them generating
Long transmission lines to distant users add cost and lose energy along the way
Sunlight in desert areas is too weak for panels to generate any electricity
questions.explanation: The cost-effective use of a renewable resource depends on transferring the energy as well as collecting it. A slightly less sunny site near users and existing lines may deliver cheaper electricity.

questions.stem: How does a pumped hydro scheme store energy?
options: It heats water in a dam using sunlight and then burns the steam in a generator
It compresses air beneath a dam until the pressure drives a set of wind turbines
It pumps water uphill when there is surplus electricity and releases it through turbines later
It stores electricity directly in the water, which glows when the energy is released
questions.explanation: Surplus electricity is stored as gravitational potential energy of water in an upper reservoir. Some energy is lost to friction and in the pumps and turbines, so less comes back than was put in.

questions.stem: A battery returns about 90% of the energy put into it, and a pumped hydro scheme about 75%. Why is pumped hydro still built for large-scale storage?
options: It can store very large amounts of energy for long periods and lasts for decades
It returns more energy than it receives, because falling water gains extra energy
It avoids all energy losses, because water does not experience any friction
It needs no suitable site, so it can be built cheaply on any flat ground
questions.explanation: Efficiency is only one constraint on cost-effective storage. Pumped hydro has a lower round-trip efficiency but can store large amounts of energy for many hours and has a long working life. It needs hills and water, so suitable sites are limited.

questions.stem: Which of these technologies typically converts the highest percentage of its input energy into electricity?
options: A hydroelectric turbine and generator
A commercial solar photovoltaic panel
A modern horizontal-axis wind turbine
A crop grown to be burnt as biomass fuel
questions.explanation: Hydroelectric generators convert well over 80% of the energy of falling water into electricity. Commercial solar panels convert about a fifth of sunlight, and wind turbines cannot exceed the Betz limit.

questions.stem: Warm groundwater pumped from deep aquifers beneath Perth is used to heat swimming pools rather than to generate electricity. Why?
options: Its temperature suits direct heating but is too low for efficient electricity generation
Its temperature is so high that it would damage any turbine used to generate electricity
It is a non-renewable fossil fuel, so it can only be burnt to heat the water
It is too salty to pass through pipes, so it is poured directly into the pools
questions.explanation: Electricity generation needs much hotter fluids than direct heating does. Using moderately warm water directly for heating is efficient, which is one reason geothermal investment depends on local geology and economics.

questions.stem: A government is deciding whether to support a geothermal power project. Which of these is a political consideration rather than an environmental or economic one?
options: The chance that injecting fluids triggers small earthquakes
The temperature of the rock at the planned drilling depth
Government renewable energy targets and policy support
The high and uncertain cost of drilling to deep hot rock
questions.explanation: Targets, subsidies and policy are political considerations. Drilling cost is economic, induced seismicity is environmental, and rock temperature is a geological fact that underlies the other decisions.

questions.stem: A company assessing a geothermal power project finds very hot rock at 4 km depth, but drilling there costs far more than expected and the site is 300 km from the nearest grid connection. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The project will be cheap, because hot rock lowers drilling costs
The project will not need transmission lines, because heat travels
The project may not be cost-effective, despite a good heat resource
The project must go ahead, because geothermal heat is renewable
questions.explanation: A good resource is not enough on its own. Drilling cost and the cost and losses of transferring energy to users can make a project uneconomic, which is why geothermal decisions weigh economic as well as environmental and political factors.
